summary: Shallow copy ({...state}) leaks player mutations to previous store state
failure_scenario: Every engine function does { ...state } but newState.players === state.players. Mutations like player.folded=true, player.chips-=amount also corrupt the old store state. If a Zustand subscriber reads store.state between get() and set() inside playerAction (e.g., via subscribe() middleware or React concurrent features), it sees partially mutated player objects with no corresponding root state update.

summary: AI decision computed from stale closure state while playerAction uses current store state
failure_scenario: Two AI turns in rapid succession: the first AI's setTimeout captures state at t=0. At t=200ms a human action changes state (new hand). At t=1000ms the old timeout fires and calls aiEngine.makeDecision with stale state (wrong player, wrong pot, wrong community cards). The decision could be Fold on a monster hand or Call on trash, then playerAction applies it to the current store state. The effect cleanup mitigates this but does not eliminate the race — the stale timeout fires during the brief window between the cleanup registration and the new effect running.

summary: getValidActionsForAI duplicates engine's getValidActions with subtle differences
failure_scenario: getValidActionsForAI (ai/types.ts:33) has a `minRaise > 0` guard for Raise that getValidActions (game/index.ts:505) lacks. getValidActions checks player.isOut but getValidActionsForAI doesn't. Any future rule change (straddle, bring-in, min-raise floor) must be updated in both locations. The AI currently shows different Raise eligibility than the human UI for the same game state — a discrepancy that will diverge further on the next rule change.

summary: showdown is a 120-line god function with 6 distinct responsibilities
failure_scenario: Pot collection, hand evaluation (all players), side-pot level calculation, leftover distribution, chip payout, winner struct construction are all in one function. The side-pot logic (lines 388-418) uses a multi-pass approach (activeBetLevels + leftover) whose correctness is hard to verify by inspection. A bug in the leftover distribution (lines 408-418) would silently misallocate chips at the table's final moment — the hardest place to debug.

summary: Dealing animation timeout reset by state changes; ActionPanel not guarded by isDealing
failure_scenario: The dealing-animation useEffect lists `state` as a dependency (line 164). If the human clicks an action button during dealing (ActionPanel is rendered at line 386 without `!isDealing` guard), `playerAction` changes state, re-fires the effect, clears and re-sets the timeout. Each click extends the dealing animation duration. In heads-up where the human is the preflop first-to-act, cards never finish animating if the human clicks repeatedly.

summary: createSimulationDeck and shuffleCards duplicate engine/deck.ts with identical logic
failure_scenario: hard.ts re-implements Fisher-Yates shuffle (lines 101-108) as shuffleCards and builds a 52-card deck from scratch in createSimulationDeck (lines 92-100). Both exist verbatim in engine/deck.ts as shuffleDeck and createDeck. If the deck structure changes (e.g., adding card metadata, changing suit/rank enums), the AI simulation silently diverges from the real deck. The Monte Carlo simulation would then evaluate impossible or incorrect hands.

summary: getSeatRole called per render per player with O(n) traversal, no memoization
failure_scenario: getSeatRole (gameTableUtils.ts:43-74) does players.findIndex(), players.filter(), indexOf(), and a while-loop walk for every player every render. For 6 players that's 6 full traversals per state change. Combined with the broad state dependency in useGameLoop (Finding 2), every chip-update triggers these traversals on every AI action. No crash, but 6× O(n) wasted work per state transition.

summary: isAnyAllIn declared in store interface and listed as effect dependency but never assigned
failure_scenario: isAnyAllIn is initialized to false (line 31) and never set() anywhere. It appears in useGameLoop's useEffect dependency array (useGameLoop.ts:58). Since it never changes, it contributes nothing to the dependency-triggering logic but makes the dependency list misleading — a future developer adding isAnyAllIn assignments would expect the effect to re-fire, but would need to verify that the current dependency-listing pattern actually picks up the change.

summary: HAND_NAMES defined locally in ResultModal duplicates canonical copy in engine/constants.ts
failure_scenario: The array ['高牌','一对',...,'皇家同花顺'] is declared in engine/constants.ts:35 (as const) and again in ResultModal.tsx:10 (as plain string[]). The local copy is only used as a fallback in getHandLabel when handResult.description is falsy — but scoreCards always sets description, so the local HAND_NAMES fallback is dead code. If the canonical list is ever reordered or renamed, the dead local copy becomes a stale maintenance artifact.

summary: Side-pot leftover distribution logic is correct by empirical testing but fragile by inspection
failure_scenario: The leftover computation (line 411) runs after the level-loop builds sidePots. If all active players bet the same amount (single level), the level-loop produces exactly one side pot and leftover should be 0. If a folded player has a bet amount between active-player levels, their surplus lands in leftover. The merge at line 413 (`sidePots[last].amount += leftover`) assumes the last pot is always the right bucket. If active players have descending totalBet (possible with fold-then-reraise), a single-level scenario could produce an empty pot list and leftover > 0, triggering the else-branch at line 416 which creates a new pot for all active players — which distributes the folded player's chips to active players who didn't cover that bet. The test suite passes, but a formal proof of correctness requires tracing the level math for every permutation of folded-vs-active totalBets.
